correctness.rationale: Directly identify the number of white neighbors of a blue rook cell with the sum of its two bipartite endpoint white degrees. This makes a force exactly a leaf-isolate incidence, while a completely white cycle remains forever unforceable. An initial leaf with opposite isolate permits one force creating isolates on both sides and then inductively peeling any remaining white forest. Two-sort bipartite Prüfer tree counts give exact sizes and leaf-side exclusions, and the labeled exponential formula with inclusion-exclusion gives every coefficient; a two-component extremal forest gives the Stirling minimum-count formula. All boundary cases m,n>=1 were checked in the proof. Standard-library direct simulation agreed for 70,502 board colorings; direct tree census covered 5,140 spanning-tree instances, and 25 larger-parameter comparisons check the extremal closed expression. No step asserts that finite tests prove the infinite theorem.

claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: Current proof supplies a necessary-and-sufficient characterization of all admissible initial subsets, a formal species identity specifying every coefficient, and a Stirling-number formula for the minimum coefficient. These do not follow from knowledge of the minimum cardinality, from a few universal coefficients, or merely from the marginal number of forts by size. Statements about other graph invariants on the same underlying rook graph do not directly yield the new zero-forcing enumerator. This is a statement-level comparison, not a title comparison.

value.rationale: The established gap is not another forcing-number substitution: it classifies every one of \(2^{mn}\) candidate initial sets on a natural two-parameter Cartesian-product family and computes the complete zero-forcing polynomial through a structured bipartite-tree component series. The Stirling expression determines the exact number of minimum sets, a previously unprovided natural multiplicity. The bridge between forcing dynamics, forests, leaves and labeled-tree enumeration is reusable and mathematically motivated; the theorem neither relies on an arbitrary finite slice nor claims a broad result for unrelated products.
